## How to follow this segment

This eight-minute segment is an instructor demonstration. Watch the
screen and answer one question with the room; you do not need to run
any code. To run the assessment yourself later, use the
[follow-up section](#fair-follow-up) at the end of this page.

## What would a collaborator need?

Allow about one minute. We use the **FAIR** principles to document the
`HealthWellbeing` teaching snapshot and assess what software can
discover about it. The table gives one question to ask for each
principle [@gofair-principles].

| Principle | Ask | Example for this dataset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Findable** | Can someone locate and identify it? | A named record with a stable identifier and searchable metadata. |
| **Accessible** | How can someone retrieve it, and on what terms? | A working download link with a statement of the access terms, or clear instructions for requesting access. |
| **Interoperable** | Can people and software interpret its structure? | Use shared metadata terms such as Schema.org and describe the variables and their units. |
| **Reusable** | Can someone judge whether it suits their project? | Explain the source, the unit of observation, and the licence. |

Access may require authentication or approval. A record can explain those
conditions while keeping the observations restricted.

## Describe the snapshot with dataspice {#create-fair-metadata}

Allow about three minutes. Four prepared CSV files under
`data/metadata/health-wellbeing/` record the title and licence, creator,
download link, and variables. The row for `n` in `attributes.csv` says
that each row of the data describes **one study** and `n` is the sample
size within that study. The teaching snapshot has 29 rows and five
variables [@healthwellbeing].

*dataspice* combines the CSV files into a Schema.org JSON-LD record
[@dataspice]. The excerpt shows the title, licence, download link, and
the entry for `n`, so you can see that its meaning and unit survive the
export.

```{r health-dataspice-export, eval = TRUE}
source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
source_dir <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing")
metadata_dir <- file.path(workshop_output_dir(), "metadata")
dir.create(metadata_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

templates <- file.path(
  source_dir, c("biblio.csv", "creators.csv", "access.csv", "attributes.csv")
)
stopifnot(all(file.copy(templates, metadata_dir, overwrite = TRUE)))
dataspice::write_spice(path = metadata_dir)

record <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(metadata_dir, "dataspice.json"))
excerpt <- record[c("name", "license", "distribution")]
excerpt$variableMeasured <- Filter(
  function(variable) variable$name == "n", record$variableMeasured
)
jsonlite::toJSON(excerpt, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
```

This record describes the [verified teaching file](00_preparation.qmd#preparation-data).
The link resolves to a particular upstream revision. Keep the
source and licence notice in `data/raw/` with the metadata.
The DOI in `biblio.csv` identifies the original review. Check for
placeholder coverage fields before publishing the generated record.

The repository's reviewed copy omits empty publication and coverage
fields, and writes `type` as `@type`; both mean the same under the
Schema.org context. The full record below comes from the same file the
assessment uses.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## HealthWellbeing JSON-LD

```{r health-jsonld-record, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = TRUE}
metadata_file <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing", "dataspice.json")
cat(c("```json", readLines(metadata_file, warn = FALSE), "```"), sep = "\n")
```
:::

## Assess the snapshot with rfair {#assess-fair-metadata}

Allow about three minutes, including 30 seconds for the question.
*rfair* takes a URL or persistent identifier and applies a set of tests
to the metadata it can retrieve [@rfair]. Before the session, the
instructor assessed the **same data file** twice:

1. **Download URL alone.** The upstream URL leads directly to the data
   file, so the assessor gets a download to check but little context
   about the dataset.
2. **With the JSON-LD supplied.** The same URL, with the record above
   supplied as a separate metadata endpoint.

In a prepared run with `rfair` 0.2.0, FAIRsFAIR metrics 0.8, and the
locally served JSON-LD, the download returned HTTP 200 in both runs.
The extra metadata supplied the title and MIT licence. One metric
from each principle shows what changed and what stayed the same.

| Metric | Download URL alone | With the JSON-LD supplied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Persistent identifier (`FsF-F1-02MD`) | Fail | Fail |
| Access information in metadata (`FsF-A1-01M`) | Fail | Fail |
| Formal language for metadata (`FsF-I1-01M`) | Fail | Pass |
| Licence in metadata (`FsF-R1.1-01M`) | Fail | Pass |

**Question for the room.** The file downloaded successfully in both
runs, yet the access check failed both times. Why? What would you add
to the public record so a reader knows how to get the file?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## One possible answer

This metric looks for access information in the metadata. A working
link shows that the assessor could download the file at that moment.
It does not tell a reader whether anyone can download it, whether
they need to sign in, or whether they must request approval.

For this snapshot, a statement such as "Public download, no sign-in
required" beside the URL would answer the question. Schema.org has
`isAccessibleForFree` and `conditionsOfAccess` properties for this.
For a restricted dataset, the record could say who may access the data
and how to request it. Rerun the assessment to check whether a
particular metric version recognises the statement.
:::

An automated check can recognise JSON-LD and find a licence field.
The data are still in an R-specific format. A reader must check the
terms and decide whether the documented measurements and study
population suit their question. A score alone cannot answer that.

## Checkpoint {#metadata-checkpoint}

- Point to the file's download URL, the definition of `n`, and the
  licence in the JSON-LD.
- Explain why a working download did not satisfy the access check,
  and what statement would.
- If you gave a colleague only the dataset link, how would they find
  the metadata the instructor supplied to *rfair*? A dataset landing
  page or repository record can expose it. The archiving segment
  returns to this question.

The record now says what the data mean and how to get them. It does
not say which version of the data produced a given result. Next, we
identify that version.
[Data and model versioning](04_versioning.qmd)

## After the workshop: run the assessment yourself {#fair-follow-up}

Run these in the **R Console** from the project root. The assessments
contact the upstream download URL, so they need network access. If a
live request fails, check `resolution` and `harvest_errors` before
interpreting the tests.

First, assess the download URL alone.

```{r health-rfair-baseline, eval = FALSE}
metadata_file <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing", "dataspice.json")
metadata <- jsonlite::read_json(metadata_file)
snapshot_url <- metadata$distribution[[1L]]$contentUrl
baseline <- rfair::assess_fair(
  snapshot_url, metric_version = "0.8", timeout = 6, max_time = 30
)
baseline$resolution[c("ok", "status")]
baseline$harvest_errors
baseline$metadata[c("title", "license")]
```

Then supply the repository's [raw JSON-LD URL](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/main/data/metadata/health-wellbeing/dataspice.json)
as a metadata endpoint. This URL works once the file reaches `main`.
To check an unpublished copy, use the local option below. Compare the
same data file under the same metric version.

```{r health-rfair-supplement, eval = FALSE}
metadata_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/main/",
  "data/metadata/health-wellbeing/dataspice.json"
)
enriched <- rfair::assess_fair(
  snapshot_url,
  metric_version = "0.8",
  metadata_service_endpoint = metadata_url,
  metadata_service_type = "schema_org",
  timeout = 6,
  max_time = 30
)
enriched$resolution[c("ok", "status")]
enriched$harvest_errors
enriched$metadata[c("title", "license")]
comparison <- rfair::fair_compare(baseline, enriched)
metrics <- c("FsF-F1-02MD", "FsF-A1-01M", "FsF-I1-01M", "FsF-R1.1-01M")
comparison[comparison$metric_identifier %in% metrics,
           c("metric_identifier", "status_a", "status_b")]
```

### Check an unpublished copy

To check the repository copy before it is on GitHub, run the following
in the RStudio **Terminal** from the project root. This example uses
Python 3 and serves only the teaching metadata directory on the local
machine.

``` bash
python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 \
  --directory data/metadata/health-wellbeing
```

In the **R Console**, run the baseline, then use this assignment in place
of the GitHub URL in the second assessment. Stop the server with
**Ctrl+C** in the Terminal when finished. The comparison still contacts
the upstream download URL.

```{r health-rfair-local-endpoint, eval = FALSE}
metadata_url <- "http://127.0.0.1:8765/dataspice.json"
```

### Save the results

To keep an example for an offline demonstration, save both assessment
objects after a successful run and load them into the console before
class. Retain the identifiers, package and metric versions, and run date
when sharing an assessment.

```{r health-rfair-save-example, eval = FALSE}
source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
metadata_dir <- file.path(workshop_output_dir(), "metadata")
dir.create(metadata_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(
  list(
    run_date = Sys.Date(),
    package_version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("rfair")),
    metric_version = "0.8",
    target = snapshot_url,
    metadata_endpoint = metadata_url,
    baseline = baseline,
    enriched = enriched
  ),
  file.path(metadata_dir, "fair-assessment.rds")
)
```
